Zinc. A transition metal with atomic number thirty, essential for biology, industry, and materials science. As a component of brass and a protective coating in galvanization, zinc prevents corrosion and is among the most widely used metals globally. Biologically, zinc is an indispensable cofactor for hundreds of enzymes and proteins, supporting immune function and wound healing.

Zinc occupies the transition metals section of the periodic table, located in Group twelve alongside cadmium and mercury. It combines with copper in varying ratios—typically sixty percent copper and forty percent zinc—to form brass, an alloy prized for its malleability, corrosion resistance, and distinctive yellow appearance. Applied as a protective coating through galvanization, zinc is submerged in molten zinc to create a layer that prevents rust and extends infrastructure lifespan in bridges, vehicles, pipes, and roofing.

As a reducing agent, zinc is highly reactive. In ozonolysis, the ozone cleavage of alkenes, zinc metallic dust decomposes ozonide intermediates and regenerates carbonyl compounds in organic synthesis. The metal melts at four hundred nineteen degrees Celsius and boils at nine hundred seven degrees. Its moderate volatility and relatively low boiling point compared to iron at two thousand eight hundred sixty-two degrees reflect its position among the transition metals.

Zinc is essential for human health. It is a cofactor for over three hundred enzymes. Deficiency causes immune suppression, hair loss, impaired wound healing, and loss of taste. Zinc is the second most abundant metal in the human body after iron. It is stored primarily in bone, muscle, and liver tissue, where it is required for protein synthesis, wound healing, immune function, and neurotransmission.

Zinc is extracted primarily from the mineral sphalerite, which is zinc sulfide, through roasting and electrolytic refining. Major producers include China, which produces twenty-eight percent of global production, as well as Peru and Australia. Zinc's electrochemical properties make it valuable as a sacrificial anode in corrosion protection systems. In dry cell batteries, specifically Leclanché cells, zinc serves as the negative electrode where it powers countless devices through chemical energy.
